abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Immunotherapy has considerably improved clinical outcomes in different types of cancers but has also been associated with the development of myocarditis, especially with that mediated by immune checkpoint inhibitors. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first cases of myocarditis after anti‐GD2 immunotherapy reported to date. We present two cases of paediatric patients who, after anti‐GD2 infusion, presented severe myocarditis with myocardial hypertrophy detected on echocardiography and confirmed with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. An increase in myocardial T1 and extracellular volume of up to 30% was observed with heterogeneous intramyocardial late enhancement. Myocarditis after anti‐GD2 immunotherapy may be more common than appreciated, occurs early after starting treatment, has a malignant course, and responds to higher steroid doses.

sec.p: Keywords: Myocarditis, Immunotherapy, Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, Corticosteroids
Revised 2023 Jan 12; Received 2022 Jun 27; Accepted 2023 Feb 7; Collection date 2023 Jun.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Immunotherapy has emerged in recent years as one of the great advances in cancer treatment. It is known that cancer is capable of manipulating immune control mechanisms to prevent an adequate response from immune cells. 1 , 2 However, immunotherapy is not exempt of side effects, immune‐related adverse events (irAE), that are also very different from those of conventional chemotherapy. The immune activation that occurs with this type of antibody can trigger an inflammatory response in any organ. Recently, in small case series, myocarditis has been identified as a side effect of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), but data on presentation, risk factors, and outcomes are limited. 3 We present the first cases of myocarditis after anti‐GD2 immunotherapy reported to date.

sec.title: Case 1

caption.p: (A) Echocardiography shows mild septal hypertrophy. (B) PET CT depicts a large right adrenal mass with high FDG uptake, corresponding with a stage 4 neuroblastoma. (C) Sinus tachycardia with T‐wave polarity changes in left precordial leads. (D) Baseline EKG. (E) Echocardiography demonstrates important increase in septal hypertrophy. (F) Peak dynamic gradient in the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) of 80 mmHg. 3‐T cardiac MR demonstrates mild increase of myocardial signal in STIR sequence (G) associated with high myocardial T1 (H, arrows; myocardial T1 at interventricular septum of 1350 msec) corresponding to mild myocardial oedema. ECV was also increase (30%) and delayed enhancement image (I) depicts heterogeneous intramyocardial late gadolinium enhancement at interventricular septum (arrow). (J) Control echocardiography, performed 20 days after the onset of symptoms, shows normalization of septal hypertrophy after treatment.

sec.title: Case 2

caption.p: (A) Echocardiography defines global myocardial hypertrophy (asterisk). (B) EKG with sinus tachycardia. 3‐T cardiac MR: short axis cine image showing mild septal hypertrophy (C, asterisk). T2 mapping image (D) demonstrates myocardial T2 of 53 msec, borderline for oedema. Myocardial T1 was high (1340 msec) in the interventricular septum (E, arrow). Delayed enhancement image (F) depicts heterogeneous intramyocardial late gadolinium enhancement at interventricular septum (arrow). Control echocardiography 13 days after the onset of symptoms (G) shows normalization of septal hypertrophy after treatment.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Autoimmune myocarditis is the most common form of cardiotoxicity observed with the use of ICIs (72%). Myocarditis is an uncommon but potentially fatal secondary effect due to the toxicity of ICIs. Although only occurring in 1% of the cases, myocarditis has the highest fatality rate (39.7%) compared with other irAEs. 4 , 5 The majority of ICI‐mediated cardiotoxicity occurs within the first 3 months of therapy, and the median time from initiation of therapy is 17–34 days. 6 Most of these patients had no prior history of cardiac disease. 7 Naxitamab is a humanized GD2‐binding monoclonal antibody. The most frequent adverse events were different than the classic ICIs: hypotension (98%), pain (96%), urticaria (83%), pyrexia (79%), bronchospasm (67%), tachycardia (63%), cough (58%), vomiting (52%), and nausea (50%). It is not usual to find adverse effects of autoimmune reactions as in classic ICIs. 8

The peculiarity of case 1 lies in the pre‐existing HCM condition, which generated diagnostic controversy as to whether there was a progression of the HCM or a myocarditis induced by immunotherapy. Cardiac MRI, response to treatment, and evolution confirmed the diagnosis of myocarditis induced by anti‐GD2 immunotherapy.

Immune‐mediated myocarditis has a highly variable clinical presentation ranging from sub‐clinical disease with asymptomatic troponin elevation to recurrent chest pain and cardiogenic shock, conduction abnormalities, leading to malignant arrhythmias and sudden death. 3 There are no guidelines for diagnosis and management of this relatively new emerging entity, and, with increasing knowledge, practice will evolve. The diagnosis of myocarditis can be very challenging and requires a very high index of clinical suspicion. ECG in a patient with myocarditis may show non‐specific findings, but a normal ECG does not rule out myocarditis. 8 , 9 Similarly, although most reported fulminant cases are associated with elevated serum troponin, an elevated troponin is not specific for myocarditis, and normal troponin, especially in cases that appear late after initiation of ICIs, does not exclude ICI‐associated myocarditis, like in case 2. An echocardiogram is a standard first‐line test for the assessment of patients, but cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) is the gold standard non‐invasive test to show signs of myocardial inflammation. The strengths of CMR include its excellent spatial resolution and its ability to provide tissue characterization with high sensitivity to detect myocardial oedema and/or fibrosis, which can be detected by CMR on T1‐weighted and T2‐weighted images. 10 , 11 This was noted in our cases with the observation of late gadolinium enhancement. A combination of these CMR criteria has a sensitivity of 76% and specificity of 96% for myocarditis. 12 The CMR‐measured myocardial native T1 value was the most robust parameter to identify myocarditis and its prognosis in patients receiving ICI therapy. 13

Corticosteroids constitute the first line of therapy for the management of most ICI‐related toxicities. 14 Timing of treatment is important given the potential for rapid progression to fulminant disease with cardiovascular compromise; therefore, prompt initiation of the immune suppression is recommended without any delay. Furthermore, cardiac symptoms should be managed according to the published guidelines from the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association.

Transient myocardial thickening should be recognized a possible presentation of acute myocarditis. We have presented two cases of myocarditis probably induced by anti‐GD2 immunotherapy, in which diagnosis was made following clinical symptoms and confirmed with non‐invasive diagnostic imaging, firstly with echocardiogram as first‐line test and later with cardiac MRI. ECG and curve of troponin levels were also helpful for diagnosis and monitoring of progression.
